shared.topic: How vaccines train the immune system

3.5.paragraph: Vaccines help the body learn to fight germs before a person gets sick. A vaccine {cont|ains} a weak or dead germ, or only a {sm|all} part of one. The body {se|es} this part and makes {spe|cial} proteins called antibodies. It {al|so} makes memory cells. These {ce|lls} remember the germ for a {lo|ng} time. Later, if the real germ {ent|ers} the body, the immune system {kn|ows} it and can fight it {qui|ckly}. Because of this, the person usually does not get very sick.

4.5.paragraph: Vaccines work by giving the immune system a safe preview of a dangerous germ. Most vaccines {con|tain} a weakened or inactivated pathogen, or just one of its {prot|eins}. When immune cells {enco|unter} this harmless version, they {pro|duce} antibodies that match its {sh|ape}. More {impor|tantly}, the body creates {mem|ory} cells that can {sur|vive} for many years. If the real pathogen {app|ears} later, these cells {reco|gnize} it and launch a much faster and stronger defense.

5.5.paragraph: Vaccination exploits the adaptive immune system's capacity to remember pathogens it has previously encountered. By {prese|nting} the body with an antigen, such as an {inact|ivated} virus or a single viral protein, a vaccine {trig|gers} the activation of B and T {lymph|ocytes} without causing {dis|ease}. Some of these cells then {differ|entiate} into long-lived memory cells. Upon {subse|quent} exposure to the genuine pathogen, these memory cells {mo|unt} a response so {ra|pid} that the infection is typically {cont|ained} before serious symptoms develop.

Dear residents,
To reduce waiting times and keep our laundry room clean, the following rules will apply starting December 1:

1. Remove your clothes within 15 minutes after a machine finishes. After 15 minutes, other residents may move your items to the folding table.

Lost items will be kept at the front desk for two weeks. If a machine is broken, please report it using the QR code on the laundry room door.

shared.title: How Dogs Became Domesticated
shared.text:
Dogs were the first animals that humans domesticated, and this happened long before people began farming. Genetic studies show that modern dogs descend from an ancient population of wolves, and most scientists believe the process began at least 15,000 years ago, when humans still lived as hunters and gatherers. But how did a dangerous predator become a loyal companion?

One popular explanation is that wolves partly domesticated themselves. Hunter-gatherer camps produced leftover food and bones, which attracted wolves. Wolves that were less fearful of people could approach the camps and eat these scraps, so they gained a steady food supply. Over many generations, these calmer animals had more offspring, and the population gradually became tamer. Humans may then have encouraged the trend by keeping the friendliest animals, which could help with hunting or warn of approaching danger.

Support for this idea comes from a long-running experiment with foxes. Researchers bred only the calmest foxes in each generation. Over the following decades, the foxes became friendly toward people, and many also developed floppy ears, curly tails, and spotted coats, traits that are common in dogs. This suggests that selecting for tameness alone can produce many of the physical changes seen in domesticated animals.

shared.title: Study abroad information session
shared.speaker: A staff member from the Study Abroad Office
shared.text: Hi, everyone. I've got a quick announcement from the Study Abroad Office. If you're thinking about spending a semester or a summer in another country, we're holding an information session next Wednesday at four o'clock in Room 210 of the student center. You'll hear from students who just came back from programs in Spain, Japan, and Ghana, and our advisors will explain how to choose a program, how your credits transfer, and what scholarships are available. Now, a lot of students think studying abroad is too expensive, but actually, many of our programs cost about the same as a semester here. Applications for next fall are due February fifteenth, so this session is a great place to start. You don't need to sign up in advance, and if you can't make it, we'll post the slides on our website the next day.

shared.question: Many elementary schools assign homework every night, while others have stopped giving homework to young children. Supporters say it builds responsibility and reinforces lessons, but critics say young children need time to play, rest, and spend time with their families. Should elementary schools give homework? Why or why not?

posts.name: Emily
posts.text: I think a small amount of homework is helpful. When I was in elementary school, a short reading or math assignment each night helped me remember what we learned in class. It also taught me to manage my time and finish tasks on my own. Those habits made middle school much easier for me.

posts.name: Daniel
posts.text: I disagree. Young children already spend six or seven hours a day in school. After that, they need time to play outside, rest, and be with their families. Also, not every child has a parent who can help at home, so homework can make the gap between students even bigger. Schools should focus on learning during class time.
